title: Expanding Expressions

findings.finding: The opening review does not rehearse multiplying two negative factors, although this is a direct step in the first worked example.
findings.breakdown: To follow −x(2y−z)=−2xy+xz, students must recognise that (−x)(−z)=xz. The review can be completed without recalling that two negative factors give a positive product.
findings.checked: p3-q1-b, d, e, f, g and i rehearse subtraction under a positive multiplier, so the candidate's claim about products with one negative factor is removed. No review item rehearses two negative factors. This is the first topic, so no preceding topic's review or exercise supplies that rehearsal. The distributive-law statement supplies the expansion method but does not rehearse signed multiplication.
findings.assumptions: Signed numerical multiplication is prior knowledge, consistent with Computation with Integers in the course library. No calculator is assumed; the missing piece is recognising the product's sign.

repair.proposal: Append two short items to the existing review: ‘Calculate: a (−3)×(−4); b (−1)×(−7).’ Expected answers: 12 and 7. These fit within the existing one-page review.

findings.doneWhen: The review checks multiplication of two negative factors before p4-example-demonstration.

findings.finding: Five complete practice tasks are repeated unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: p5-q1-j repeats p5-q1-a; p5-q1-t repeats p5-q1-k; p5-q2-j repeats p5-q2-a; p5-q2-t repeats p5-q2-k; and p7-q5-b repeats p7-q5-a.
findings.checked: Each pair has the same governing instruction, expression, values and required response. The p7 pair also has identical blank positions. None has additional givens or diagrams, and no supplied instruction assigns the repetitions a retrieval or comparison purpose. Removing the later copies preserves the surrounding variations in signs, order, coefficients and variables.
findings.assumptions: The separately labelled parts are assigned tasks; no additional explicit instructional purpose is supplied.

repair.proposal: Remove p5-q1-j, p5-q1-t, p5-q2-j, p5-q2-t and p7-q5-b.

findings.doneWhen: Each of the five unchanged tasks appears once, with the surrounding variation sequences retained.

findings.finding: An optional identity task can consolidate the relationship between a negative outside multiplier and reversing an inside subtraction.
findings.breakdown: Students explain the sign-and-order structure using distribution rather than completing another routine expansion.
findings.checked: For all real a, b and c, −a(b−c)=−ab+ac=a(c−b). The proposed addition identity is false in general: a=b=c=1 gives −2 and 2. Distribution and signed products are available by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: Variables represent real numbers. The task is optional for early finishers.

repair.proposal: After p7-q5, ask: ‘A student claims −a(b−c)=a(c−b) for all real a, b and c. Is this always true? Expand both sides to explain. Does −a(b+c)=a(c+b) also hold for every choice of values? Explain or give a counterexample.’ Expected answer: the first identity is always true because both sides equal −ab+ac; the second is false, for example when a=b=c=1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks students to justify the subtraction identity and disprove the proposed addition identity.

findings.finding: An optional task can generalise the cancellation and missing-coefficient structure in p15-q11-root.
findings.breakdown: Students determine when expansion produces a constant, then distinguish one prescribed constant from any constant.
findings.checked: Expansion gives (10+c)x+5+cd. Equality to −1 for every real x requires c=−10 and d=3/5. The expression is constant precisely when c=−10, with any real d, and then equals 5−10d. Expansion, collecting terms and determining unknown coefficients are available by this point, including in p15-q11-root.
findings.assumptions: c and d are real constants; the equality must hold for every real x. The task is optional for early finishers.

repair.proposal: After p15-q11-root, ask: ‘For 5(2x+1)+c(x+d), find every pair of real constants c and d that makes the expression equal to −1 for every x. Explain why your values work. Then describe all pairs that make the expression constant.’ Expected answer: c=−10 and d=3/5 for −1; c=−10 with any real d for a constant, whose value is 5−10d.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task explicitly distinguishes an identity for every x from an equation at one value of x.

findings.finding: A short sequence with fixed constant magnitudes and changing signs can expose how the constant and linear terms arise.
findings.breakdown: The constant term depends on one product, while the linear coefficient depends on the sum of two products.
findings.checked: The four expansions are x²+7x+10, x²+3x−10, x²−3x−10 and x²−7x+10. The follow-up expands to 2x²+5x−12. These require only signed distribution and collecting like terms, already taught. The supplied binomial practice does not contain this fixed-magnitude sign sequence.
findings.assumptions: x is real. Students predict the signs of coefficients, independently of the value of x.

repair.proposal: After p19-q2-c and before p19-q3, ask students to predict the constant term's sign and the x coefficient's sign before expanding: (x+2)(x+5); (x−2)(x+5); (x+2)(x−5); (x−2)(x−5). Keep the magnitudes 2 and 5 and both leading coefficients fixed; vary only the constant signs. Expected expansions: x²+7x+10; x²+3x−10; x²−3x−10; x²−7x+10. Ask: ‘Which two products determine the coefficient of x?’ Follow with the unpatterned question (2x−3)(x+4), whose expansion is 2x²+5x−12.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict before expanding, identify the two contributions to the linear coefficient, and apply the method to the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: One optional generalisation can ask when a monic binomial product has no linear term.
findings.breakdown: Both candidates propose the same cancellation task. A single placement is sufficient.
findings.checked: For real constants a and b, (x+a)(x+b)=x²+(a+b)x+ab. The linear term disappears exactly when a+b=0, giving b=−a and x²−a². Thus (x+7)(x−7)=x²−49. The area-model topic already supplies the four products and collection of like terms; the later rule topic supplies the same method.
findings.assumptions: a and b are real constants. The task concerns the linear coefficient in the expanded expression and is optional for early finishers.

repair.proposal: Place this task once, after p19-q3-b: ‘Expand (x+a)(x+b). What relationship between a and b makes the x term disappear? Explain why, and use your result to expand (x+7)(x−7).’ Expected answer: x²+(a+b)x+ab; a+b=0, so b=−a and the product becomes x²−a²; the example gives x²−49. This also fulfils the identical extension proposed for p22-q3-f.

findings.doneWhen: A single optional task asks students to derive the cancellation condition and apply it to an example.
